about: Each choir part's chorister drawn as weights over the speakers (speakers.json) its voice type is made from (native/vocaltract/sing-score.mjs): each speaker's weight its preset's here times a draw from the singer's seed (an exponential draw each: a seeded point of the simplex the preset weighs), so that no two singers of a part are alike where its type has more than one speaker. Presets of weights only, as the owner approved them (research/VOCALWIND_CHOIR.md, "Continuous reshaping": "sex, age and voice type are presets of weights and measures, never an axis built in"); the measures by voice type are `bodies`, below. The women's parts have one measured woman to be drawn from, W02.

bodies.about: A chorister's body within its voice type's measured spread (src/singers.rs; the owner, 16 November 2026: "have VocalWind support realistic physiological variation (even if small, to begin with) from singer to singer (women and men), supported by the literature we have"; research/VOCALWIND_CHOIR.md, "Singers drawn by voice type"). Its body (the speakers its preset weighs) is taken to stand for its group's mean; its pharynx and larynx (2.4's H0 and H1) are scaled by its type's: one plus the type's median tract length less its group's mean, over its group's mean pharynx (atlas to glottis), as the types differ mostly there; its tract's lengths (H0, H1 and the hard palate's, W1) by one plus a draw times its group's `tract_spread`; its folds (its glottis's rest length; its rest F0 inversely) by its type's mean fold length plus a draw times `fold_sd_mm`, over its group's. Each draw a quantile, taken within `within` of the standard normal.

female singers.source: Roers, Mürbe & Sundberg 2009 (J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 125(1), 503-512, doi:10.1121/1.3026326): the 25 women whose whole tract was measurable, its mean (their text) and their atlas-glottis distance's (Fig. 5, read by eye); their folds' mean the six types' in Roers, Mürbe & Sundberg 2009 (J. Voice 23(4), 408-413, doi:10.1016/j.jvoice.2007.12.003, Table 3, from the trachea's diameter) weighed by its 71 women; the spread Fitch & Giedd 1999 (J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 106(3), 1511-1522, doi:10.1121/1.427148, Table I: women aged 19 to 25, 138.8 mm, s.d. 3.4, by MRI)

male singers.source: As for the women: Roers et al.'s 34 men, their atlas-glottis distance by eye (Fig. 5), their folds weighed by its 61 men; Fitch & Giedd's men aged 19 to 25, 155.4 mm, s.d. 4.4

bodies.types_source: Roers, Mürbe & Sundberg 2009: the tract's median by type (J. Acoust. Soc. Am., Fig. 4, read by eye: three straight lines, incisors to the eighth molar, to the second vertebra, to the larynx's prominence, at rest); the folds' mean by type (J. Voice, Table 3, from the trachea's greatest sagittal diameter) and their standard deviation, that diameter's (Fig. 4, read by eye) times the slope relating the two, 0.98 (Table 2)

reach.about: How far each speaker's pharynx and larynx (2.4's H0 and H1, together) may be made longer or shorter than its own in each language, measured on the engine (16 November 2026; examples/singer_reach.rs reach, on the speaker's body made by vtl-blend to sing the language, the tract mended): from 0.80 to 1.20 times its own by 0.02, its hard palate at the shortest and the longest its group's tract is drawn, every vowel the language is measured to sing (languages/vowel-places.json; blend::language_shapes) keeping at least half its own least area (carry::least_closable_area). Its reach the ratios that pass around 1 (0.80 the least tried); a speaker not given in a language is held at its own pharynx there, its tract not drawn. Lengthened, [i] closes first, the tongue body's height scaled with the pharynx's by 2.4's setFor under a palate that is not (research/MODELING_GAPS.md, "A singer's pharynx beyond its speaker's reach"); in English, W02's and JD2's [ɔ] closes at their own pharynx with the shorter mouth and by turns along it, so that neither has a reach there.
